description: Software engineer passionate about AI, healthcare, and space exploration. I'm developing AstroMed, an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring app that tracks vital signs and identifies potential health risks during space missions.
summary: AstroMed is a visual health self-assessment app for astronauts. On the way to Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 24 minutes each way, so crews must check their own health and act first. Astronauts log vitals, sleep, food, exercise, mood and symptoms in under a minute, or run guided checkups built for space: a reaction-time test, a cabin air check, an Amsler grid vision check, balance after landing, and a check for the bends after spacewalks. Every reading is compared with the astronaut’s own normal range and explained using their own data. Each result gets one of four urgency levels worded for their distance from Earth, from self-care to contacting the flight surgeon now. AstroMed also tracks prescribed medicines and whether they help, plans meals from food on board, and covers NASA’s 5 hazards and 17 spaceflight risks. Every threshold and tip cites NASA standards, NASA research or peer-reviewed studies. It works on phones and offline, keeps data private, and never prescribes. The next crews will be their own first line of care.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?
AstroMed is a health self-assessment app for astronauts. After every check-in it answers three questions: is this normal for me, here, and what should I do now?

  1. Log: record vitals, oxygen, sleep, food, water, exercise, weight, mood, stress and symptoms in under a minute. Readings can also come from a photo of a device screen (read on the device), a smartwatch CSV or a lab report.
    • vital signs;
    • NASA’s 3-minute PVT-B reaction-time test;
    • cabin CO₂, temperature and noise against NASA limits;
    • an Amsler grid for eye changes (SANS);
    • a balance and stand-up test after landing;
    • an after-spacewalk check for the bends;
    • a weekly immune and infection check.
    • Overall status: the astronaut’s health over the last 7 or 30 days, split into Physical, Mental and Routine, each marked good, worth watching or needing attention.
    • Ranked suggestions: what to do first, each with the reason from their own data and a NASA citation (for example, “you ate 80% of your energy need on 7 of 7 days”).
    • Area detail: vital averages, sleep, energy and weight trends, mood and journal patterns, doses taken, reminders done and checkups due.
    • Questions for the flight surgeon: a ready list drawn from the data (for example, a vision change or a medicine that isn’t helping).
    • Print: the summary can be printed to bring to a medical conference.

Every threshold and tip is a fixed rule cited to the exact page of NASA-STD-3001, a NASA Human Research Program evidence report, or a peer-reviewed study. 115 automated tests check the safety rules.

Benefits

  • Clear guidance when the ground is minutes away.
  • Problems caught early from your own trends.
  • Reminders, dose tracking and meal planning.
  • Ready-made reports and questions for the flight surgeon.

Intended impact
Make astronauts confident first responders for their own health on Moon and Mars missions. The same tool could serve analog missions (Antarctic stations, HERA, CHAPEA) and people on Earth far from care.

How is it creative?

  • Advice changes with distance from Earth.
  • Explanations come from your own data, not generic warnings.
  • Space self-tests run on a phone.
  • “Is my medicine working?” compares readings before and after starting.
  • Meal plans use the food actually on board.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: no diagnosis or prescribing; emergencies always escalate.
  • Evidence: every number cited and checked against its source.
  • Privacy: each person sees only their own data.
  • Cost: no paid AI.
  • Accessibility: colour paired with an icon and a label; keyboard support.
  • Mission reality: offline use, signal delay, weightlessness.

Tech stack
TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Supabase (Postgres with row-level security, sign-in, private storage), Vercel, tesseract.js (on-device text reading), Zod, Vitest (115 safety tests). An installable, offline-capable web app; no special hardware needed.

Project Links: https://astro-med-two.vercel.app

(Try the demo on the home page. No sign-in or password is needed.)

Other links:

  • About, data sources and AI use: https://astro-med-two.vercel.app/about (public, no sign-in)
  • Source code: https://github.com/SrijaDasgupta/AstroMed

AI tools

  • Claude Code (Anthropic): coding, debugging, drafting ppt; all of it reviewed and tested by me.
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI): two illustrations, labelled “AI-generated image (ChatGPT)” in the app.
  • In the app: advice comes from fixed, cited rules, not AI. An optional photo analysis uses the astronaut’s own AI key.
  • Idea and decisions: my own.

Challenges we faced

  • Free hosting limits: AstroMed runs on Supabase’s free plan, which pauses a project after a period of inactivity and caps storage. A real mission would need a paid, always-on plan.
  • No built-in AI agent: an AI assistant inside the app would need a paid AI subscription. To keep the project free, AstroMed uses cited rules instead, and the optional AI photo analysis only runs with the astronaut’s own key.
  • Health data rules: detailed diagnoses and clinical alerts on real health data would need medical-device clearance and health-data compliance (for example FDA and HIPAA in the U.S.). So AstroMed stays a self-assessment tool: it tracks, explains and advises when to contact the flight surgeon, but never diagnoses or prescribes.

What’s next

  • Validation with flight surgeons and analog missions.
  • Sync with wearables and onboard devices.
  • A crew medical officer dashboard, with consent.
  • Guided ultrasound self-scans for hidden risks.
  • More languages, and use on Earth for people far from care.

Additional facts

  • Coverage: about 80 NASA-listed conditions, all 5 hazards and 17 NASA risks, plus hidden risks (neck-vein clots, SANS, virus reactivation, space anemia, kidney stones). 5 mission environments and 12 health indicators.
  • Medicines: added only once the dose is confirmed with a doctor; flexible schedules, reminders, side effects and an “is it helping?” check.
    • Demo: a sample Mars mission, no account needed, kept in the browser for 7 days.
    • Signed in: private storage for at least 5 years, with full data export.
